## Simple explanation

Perplexity measures how surprised a language model is by text. Lower
perplexity means the model assigned higher probability to the observed
tokens, under the specific evaluation setup.

## Technical explanation

For tokens $x_1,\ldots,x_N$, perplexity is commonly defined as
$\exp(-\frac{1}{N}\sum_i \log p(x_i\mid x_{<i}))$. It is the exponential of
average token-level negative log-likelihood, with the log base and
tokenization convention handled consistently.

## Why it matters in AI engineering

Perplexity is useful for comparing language models on the same corpus and
tokenization setup. It is not a complete measure of usefulness, factuality,
or task performance, and scores can be incomparable across differing
tokenizers or evaluation procedures.

## How it works

The model predicts each next token from its preceding context. Evaluation
collects the probability assigned to the actual next token, averages the
negative log probabilities, and exponentiates that average. For long
sequences, implementations often use a sliding context window.

## Practical example

To compare two versions of the same model, evaluate each on the same
held-out text, with identical tokenization and context handling. If one
assigns greater probability to the observed tokens on average, its
perplexity is lower, but task-specific evaluation is still needed.

## Common misconceptions

- Lower perplexity does not guarantee better answers to user questions.
- Perplexity values depend on tokenization, data, and evaluation details;
  scores from different setups should not be compared casually.
